Neurology · published research

Stress

In chronically stressed mice, brain-gut PBM improved cognitive outcomes and changed hippocampal Sirt1 and inflammatory measures. In a surgical-stress rat model, PBM reduced hippocampal p53, but behavioral outcomes were not reported.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In chronically stressed mice, brain-gut PBM improved cognitive outcomes and changed hippocampal Sirt1 and inflammatory measures. In a surgical-stress rat model, PBM reduced hippocampal p53, but behavioral outcomes were not reported.

Summary of the Evidence

This narrow mapping contains four unique titles: two animal studies and two broad mechanistic reviews. The primary studies model chronic mild stress in mice and surgical stress in rats, rather than one shared clinical stress condition. The two reviews were mapped from a broader homeostasis-and-stress category and do not add experimental cohorts. Oxidative-stress records from disease-specific categories were excluded.

Human and clinical evidence

No human treatment study for perceived stress, chronic stress or a defined stress-related disorder was identified in the mapped set.

Animal evidence

Sancho-Balsells et al. reported that brain-gut PBM improved cognitive outcomes in chronically stressed mice and changed hippocampal Sirt1, neuroinflammatory and microbiome measures (Sancho-Balsells et al. 2024). In a rat model using septoplasty to induce surgical stress, PBM reduced hippocampal p53 expression, but behavioral outcomes were not measured (Kotov et al. 2025). These are distinct animal contexts, and the marker change in the surgical model is not evidence that perceived stress improved.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo stress study was identified. The two mapped reviews discuss signaling pathways but do not supply separate cell or tissue cohorts.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The mouse publication describes a brain-gut PBM approach, while the rat report treats a surgical-stress model. The source records do not provide a complete common set of wavelengths, dose, exposure duration and schedule across both studies. These interventions may act through different targets, and neither procedure can be assumed to represent a standard stress treatment in people.

Interpretation

The evidence supports a possible effect on selected cognitive or tissue measures in two animal models. It does not show relief of human stress symptoms, anxiety or functional impairment. The different models, sparse primary evidence and lack of patient outcomes are the main reasons the finding remains uncertain.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for reducing stress in people because the evidence includes two animal experiments and two broad mechanistic reviews. Low within the mouse model for selected cognition and inflammatory outcomes.
Publications and records4 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The mouse and rat studies model different contexts, and the two mapped reviews discuss broad stress-related mechanisms rather than clinical stress outcomes. No patient report was identified. A human study should define the stress-related condition, measure perceived symptoms and functioning, and test one clearly specified PBM route against sham.
